parts.text:
A curve has equation
$x^2+2xy-3y^2+16=0$.
Find the coordinates of the points on the curve where $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1 (A1) A1: $2x+(2x\frac{dy}{dx}+2y)-6y\frac{dy}{dx}=0$
M1: $\frac{dy}{dx}=0 \Rightarrow x+y=0$ or equivalent
Note: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x+y}{3y-x}$
M1: Eliminating either variable and solving for at least one value of $x$ or $y$.
$y^2-2y^2-3y^2+16=0$ or the same equation in $x$
A1: $y=\pm 2$ or $x=\pm 2$
A1: $(2,-2), (-2,2)$

Alternative
$3y^2-2xy-(x^2+16)=0$
$y=\frac{2x\pm\sqrt{(16x^2+192)}}{6}$
M1 A1$\pm$ A1: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{3}\pm\frac{1}{3}.\frac{8x}{\sqrt{(16x^2+192)}}$
M1: $\frac{dy}{dx}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{8x}{\sqrt{(16x^2+192)}}=\pm 1$
M1 A1: $64x^2=16x^2+192$, $x=\pm 2$
A1: $(2,-2), (-2,2)$

parts.text:
Use the substitution $x=\sin\theta$ to find the exact value of
$\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \frac{1}{(1-x^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\,dx$.
(7)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $\int \frac{1}{(1-x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\,dx=\int \frac{1}{(1-\sin^2\theta)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\cos\theta\,d\theta$ Use of $x=\sin\theta$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta}=\cos\theta$
M1 A1: $=\int \frac{1}{\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta$
M1 A1: $=\int \sec^2\theta\,d\theta=\tan\theta$
M1: Using the limits 0 and $\frac{\pi}{6}$ to evaluate integral
A1: $[\tan\theta]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$ $\left(=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)$ cao

Alternative for final M1 A1
Returning to the variable $x$ and using the limits 0 and $\frac{1}{2}$ to evaluate integral
M1: $\left[\frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}}\right]_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$
A1: $\left(=\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)$ cao

questions.stem:
Figure 1
Figure 1 shows the graph of the curve with equation
$y=xe^{2x}$, $x\geqslant 0$.
The finite region $R$ bounded by the lines $x=1$, the $x$-axis and the curve is shown shaded in Figure 1.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Use integration to find the exact value of the area for $R$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1 A1: $\int xe^{2x}\,dx=\frac{1}{2}xe^{2x}-\frac{1}{2}\int e^{2x}\,dx$ Attempting parts in the right direction
A1: $=\frac{1}{2}xe^{2x}-\frac{1}{4}e^{2x}$
M1 A1: $\left[\frac{1}{2}xe^{2x}-\frac{1}{4}e^{2x}\right]_{0}^{1}=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}e^2$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Complete the table with the values of $y$ corresponding to $x=0.4$ and $0.8$.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline x & 0 & 0.2 & 0.4 & 0.6 & 0.8 & 1\\ \hline y=xe^{2x} & 0 & 0.29836 & & 1.99207 & & 7.38906\\ \hline\end{array}$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: $x=0.4 \Rightarrow y\approx 0.89022$; $x=0.8 \Rightarrow y\approx 3.96243$ Both are required to 5 d.p

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Use the trapezium rule with all the values in the table to find an approximate value for this area, giving your answer to 4 significant figures.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: $I\approx \frac{1}{2}\times 0.2\times[...]$
M1 A1ft: $\approx ...\times[0+7.38906+2(0.29836+.89022+1.99207+3.96243)]$ ft their answers to (b)
$\approx 0.1\times 21.67522$
A1: $\approx 2.168$ cao
Note $\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}e^2\approx 2.097...$

questions.stem:
A curve has parametric equations
$x=2\cot t$, $y=2\sin^2 t$, $0<t\leqslant \frac{\pi}{2}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find an expression for $\frac{dy}{dx}$ in terms of the parameter $t$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1 A1: $\frac{dx}{dt}=-2\csc^2 t$, $\frac{dy}{dt}=4\sin t\cos t$ both
M1 A1: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{-2\sin t\cos t}{\csc^2 t}$ $\left(=-2\sin^3 t\cos t\right)$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find an equation of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi}{4}$.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: At $t=\frac{\pi}{4}$, $x=2$, $y=1$ both $x$ and $y$
M1: Substitutes $t=\frac{\pi}{4}$ into an attempt at $\frac{dy}{dx}$ to obtain gradient $\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)$
M1 A1: Equation of tangent is $y-1=-\frac{1}{2}(x-2)$
Accept $x+2y=4$ or any correct equivalent

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find a cartesian equation of the curve in the form $y=\mathrm{f}(x)$. State the domain on which the curve is defined.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Uses $1+\cot^2 t=\csc^2 t$, or equivalent, to eliminate $t$
A1: $1+\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^2=\frac{2}{y}$ correctly eliminates $t$
A1: $y=\frac{8}{4+x^2}$ cao
B1: The domain is $x\geqslant 0$

An alternative in (c)
$\sin t=\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$; $\cos t=\frac{x}{2}\sin t=\frac{x}{2}\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$
M1 A1: $\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t=1 \Rightarrow \frac{y}{2}+\frac{x^2}{4}\times\frac{y}{2}=1$
A1: Leading to $y=\frac{8}{4+x^2}$

questions.stem: Liquid is pouring into a container at a constant rate of $20\,\mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}$ and is leaking out at a rate proportional to the volume of the liquid already in the container.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Explain why, at time $t$ seconds, the volume, $V\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, of liquid in the container satisfies the differential equation
$\frac{dV}{dt}=20-kV$,
where $k$ is a positive constant.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: $\frac{dV}{dt}$ is the rate of increase of volume (with respect to time)
B1: $-kV$: $k$ is constant of proportionality and the negative shows decrease (or loss) giving $\frac{dV}{dt}=20-kV$ * These Bs are to be awarded independently

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The container is initially empty.
(b) By solving the differential equation, show that
$V=A+Be^{-kt}$,
giving the values of $A$ and $B$ in terms of $k$.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $\int \frac{1}{20-kV}\,dV=\int 1\,dt$ separating variables
M1 A1: $-\frac{1}{k}\ln(20-kV)=t$ (+C)
M1: Using $V=0, t=0$ to evaluate the constant of integration
$c=-\frac{1}{k}\ln 20$
$t=\frac{1}{k}\ln\left(\frac{20}{20-kV}\right)$
M1: Obtaining answer in the form $V=A+Be^{-kt}$
A1: $V=\frac{20}{k}-\frac{20}{k}e^{-kt}$ Accept $\frac{20}{k}(1-e^{-kt})$

Alternative to (b)
Using printed answer and differentiating $\frac{dV}{dt}=-kBe^{-kt}$
M1: Substituting into differential equation
$-kBe^{-kt}=20-kA-kBe^{-kt}$
M1 A1: $A=\frac{20}{k}$
M1: Using $V=0, t=0$ in printed answer to obtain $A+B=0$
A1: $B=-\frac{20}{k}$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Given also that $\frac{dV}{dt}=10$ when $t=5$,
(c) find the volume of liquid in the container at 10 s after the start.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $\frac{dV}{dt}=20e^{-kt}$ Can be implied
M1 A1: $\frac{dV}{dt}=10, t=5 \Rightarrow 10=20e^{-kt} \Rightarrow k=\frac{1}{5}\ln 2\approx 0.139$
M1 A1: At $t=10$, $V=\frac{75}{\ln 2}$ awrt 108

parts.reason: Vector equation of a line and intersection of lines are explicitly listed as concepts no 9MA0 statement covers, so this is out.

parts.reason: Scalar (dot) product and angle between lines are explicitly excluded concepts not covered by any 9MA0 statement.

parts.reason: Although magnitude/distance of vectors is ordinary in-spec vector work (P10.2/P10.4), this part requires the point B found in part (a) via line intersection, which is out-of-spec; the part only makes sense after using that out-of-spec answer.
